questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply naive bayes to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Read 0.6 and 0.5 with 0.3 first: a naive Bayes classifier has class prior 0.6. Given two observed features, the class-conditional likelihoods for the positive class are 0.5 and 0.6, and for the negative class they are 0.5 and 0.3. What is the posterior probability of the positive class, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Uses a single likelihood and ignores the other evidence
Reports the prior and ignores the observed features
Reports the unnormalized numerator as if it were a posterior

questions.explanation: Naive Bayes multiplies likelihoods under the conditional-independence assumption: the positive score is 0.6*0.5*0.6 = 0.18 and the negative score is (1-0.6)*0.5*0.3 = 0.06. Normalizing gives 0.75. The numerator alone is not normalized, one likelihood discards evidence, and the prior ignores the features entirely.
questions.hint: Multiply each class's prior by its likelihoods, then normalize across classes.

Computes entropy instead of Gini impurity
Reports purity, the complement of Gini impurity

Flips the sign of the step function output

Sums successor values instead of taking the maximum
Uses the first successor value instead of the maximum

Lowering the threshold produces the opposite pattern, and the two metrics do trade off, so they cannot both move together or stay fixed in general.
questions.hint: Consider which predictions are relabeled when the cutoff moves upward.

questions.learningObjective: Apply intelligent agents to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Suppose the values are 11, 2, and 3; a performance measure awards +11 points for each correctly filed document, subtracts 2 for each misfiled document, and subtracts 3 for each second of delay. An agent files 6 documents correctly, misfiles 1, and finishes in 2 seconds. What total score does the performance measure assign to this behavior?

options.misconception: Adds the misplacement penalty rather than subtracting it
Counts misplaced items as if they were correctly sorted
Treats delay cost as a reward instead of a penalty

questions.explanation: The measure sums three signed contributions: +11 times 6 correctly filed documents gives 66, minus 2 times 1 misfiles gives -2, and minus 3 times 2 seconds gives -6. The total 66 - 2 - 6 = 58 rewards correctness and penalizes both errors and delay. Adding the delay term, adding the misfiles, or crediting misfiles as correct all invert the intended penalties, so those totals are wrong.
questions.hint: Write each contribution with its sign, then add the three products.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply problem formulation to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Considering problem formulation, case 2688 — a cleaning robot maps a room but cannot observe furniture that family members move after it looks away. Its wheel commands have perfectly predictable effects, yet the room layout keeps changing while it works and positions vary over a continuum. Which set of environment properties best characterizes this task? Identify the right answer, carefully.

options.text: Partially observable, stochastic, static, continuous.
options.misconception: Mistakes unseen changes for random action outcomes.

options.text: Partially observable, deterministic, static, discrete.
options.misconception: Ignores both passing time and continuous positions.

options.text: Fully observable, deterministic, dynamic, continuous.
options.misconception: Wrongly grants the agent complete state information.

options.text: Partially observable, deterministic, dynamic, continuous.

questions.explanation: The robot cannot see every relevant fact, so the environment is partially observable. Actions have perfectly predictable effects, so it is deterministic. The layout changes while the agent deliberates, so it is dynamic. Positions range over a continuum, so it is continuous. Each competing option flips one of these four properties and therefore misdescribes the task.
questions.hint: Check observability, action predictability, change over time, and whether the state space is discrete.

questions.stem: Considering agent designs, case 2689 — an agent selects each action using only the percept it receives at this instant. It keeps no record of earlier observations and builds no model of how the environment evolves. Which agent design does this description match? Identify the right answer, carefully.

options.text: A goal-based agent planning toward a target state.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes explicit goals and lookahead search.

options.text: A utility-based agent maximizing expected satisfaction.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes a utility function over outcomes.

options.text: A model-based reflex agent tracking hidden state.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes the agent maintains any state at all.

options.text: A simple reflex agent acting only on the current percept.

questions.explanation: A simple reflex agent maps the current percept directly to an action through condition-action rules, with no memory or world model. The description explicitly denies stored history and an environment model, ruling out model-based, goal-based, and utility-based designs, each of which needs internal state beyond the present percept.
questions.hint: Ask whether the agent stores anything beyond the percept in front of it.

questions.learningObjective: Apply heuristics to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: With the data 0 / 11 / 6 in view, on a four-connected grid an agent starts at (0, 0) and must reach a goal at (11, 6). Each unit step costs 1 and no obstacles are present. What is the Manhattan-distance heuristic value at the starting state?

options.misconception: Uses the area of the rectangle instead of step distance
Counts only the larger coordinate displacement
Undercounts by assuming the goal square needs no move

questions.explanation: Manhattan distance adds the absolute coordinate differences: |11 - 0| + |6 - 0| = 11 + 6 = 17. Because there are no diagonal moves, this is also the exact optimal path cost. Multiplying coordinates, dropping one step, or keeping only the larger displacement each fails to sum both coordinate gaps and so understates the distance.
questions.hint: Sum the horizontal and vertical separations independently.

questions.learningObjective: Apply adversarial search to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: With the data 8 / 5 / 1 in view, a two-ply game tree has a MAX root with two MIN children. The first MIN child has leaves 8 and 5; the second MIN child has leaves 1 and 3. Under minimax with both players choosing optimally, what value is backed up to the root?

options.misconception: Assumes MAX gets to pick a leaf directly
Assumes MIN chooses at the root
Swaps the roles of MAX and MIN at the two levels

questions.explanation: Minimax backs up values from the leaves. Each MIN child takes the smaller of its leaves, giving 5 and 1. The MAX root then takes the larger of those, 5. Taking maxima at the MIN level swaps the players, while taking a global maximum or minimum ignores the alternating levels entirely, so each of those answers misapplies the recurrence.
questions.hint: Evaluate the bottom MIN nodes first, then let the root MAX choose between them.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply informed search to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Reviewing informed search, item 2692: a heuristic h satisfies h(n) <= h*(n) for every state n, where h*(n) is the true optimal cost from n to a goal. Which property does h necessarily have? Identify the right answer, carefully.

options.text: Monotone: its value never decreases along a path.
options.misconception: Wrongly states the opposite of the usual monotonicity direction.

options.text: Optimal: it guarantees the best path without any search.
options.misconception: Wrongly claims a bound alone searches the space.

options.text: Consistent: it obeys the triangle inequality on every arc.
options.misconception: Wrongly names the stronger arcwise condition.

options.text: Admissible: it never overestimates the true cost to the goal.

questions.explanation: The inequality h(n) <= h*(n) is exactly the definition of admissibility: the estimate never overestimates the remaining cost. Consistency is a stronger condition involving arc costs between neighboring states, and a heuristic being admissible does not by itself make search instantaneous or optimal without the surrounding algorithm guarantees. The competing options name different or invented properties.
questions.hint: Compare the estimate to the true remaining cost, not to neighbor costs.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply bayesian inference to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Building on 0.16 and 0.82, then 0.7, a disease has prevalence 0.16. A test detects it with sensitivity 0.82 when present and has specificity 0.7 when absent. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability, to four decimals, that this person actually has the disease?

options.misconception: Reports the prior probability of disease
Reports only the joint numerator, unnormalized
Reports sensitivity and ignores the base rate

questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem gives P(D|+) = se*p / (se*p + (1 - sp)*(1 - p)) = 0.131 / (0.131 + 0.252) = 0.3424. The numerator alone is not a probability because it is unnormalized, and the sensitivity or the prior each ignore the false-positive contributions and the base rate, which is precisely the base-rate fallacy.
questions.hint: Compute true positives and false positives over a population, then take the true-positive share.

questions.stem: Building on 0.7 and 0.5, then 0.1, in a Bayesian network with edge A -> B, the prior is P(A) = 0.7. The conditional table gives P(B | A) = 0.5 and P(B | not A) = 0.1. What is the joint probability P(A and B), to four decimals?

options.misconception: Computes the marginal probability of the child instead
Reports the conditional probability and ignores the parent
Uses the conditional probability of the wrong parent state

questions.explanation: The joint distribution factorizes as P(A, B) = P(A) * P(B | A) = 0.7 * 0.5 = 0.35. Adding the contribution from not A computes the marginal P(B), and using P(B | not A) or the conditional alone does not follow the factorization for the event A and B together.
questions.hint: Multiply the parent's prior by the child's conditional given that parent state.

questions.learningObjective: Apply propositional logic to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: An instance of propositional logic, no. 2695: given the truth assignment P = true, Q = false, R = false, evaluate the propositional formula (P and Q) or (not P and R). Which statement is correct? Report the result, precisely.

options.text: True, but only when R is false.
options.misconception: Wrongly ties the value to R rather than to the disjuncts.

options.text: Undetermined without knowing Q and R together.
options.misconception: Wrongly claims the truth value cannot be evaluated.

options.text: True, because at least one disjunct holds.
options.misconception: Reverses the truth value of the disjunction.

options.text: False, because neither disjunct holds.

questions.explanation: With P = true and Q = false, the first conjunct P and Q is false. With not P = false and R = false, the second conjunct is false. The disjunction of false and false is false, so neither disjunct holds. The alternatives either invert the result or wrongly claim the value is undecidable when all atoms are assigned.
questions.hint: Evaluate each conjunction first, then combine them with or.

Off-by-one error in the subtraction
Counts the test partition instead of the training partition

questions.stem: Read 4 and 2 with 0.05 first: for the loss L(w) = (w - 4)^2, gradient descent uses learning rate 0.05 from starting weight w = 7. The derivative is dL/dw = 2(w - 4). What is the weight after one update step, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Drops the factor of two from the derivative
Ignores the learning rate entirely
Performs gradient ascent by flipping the update sign

questions.explanation: The gradient at w = 7 is 2(7 - 4) = 6. The descent update is w - lr * grad = 7 - 0.05 * (6) = 6.7. Adding the gradient instead ascends the loss, dropping the factor of two uses the wrong derivative, and omitting the learning rate takes a full-size step, so each alternative is a distinct calculus or step-size error.
questions.hint: Substitute w into 2(w - target), then move opposite the gradient by lr times that value.

questions.learningObjective: Apply regression metrics to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: A regressor predicts 8, 5, 1 for three examples whose true targets are 3, 7, 1. What is the mean squared error of these predictions, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Forgets to divide by the number of examples
Corrupts the first residual by adding instead of subtracting
Uses mean absolute error instead of squared error

questions.explanation: The squared residuals are (8 - 3)^2, (5 - 7)^2, and (1 - 1)^2, summing to 29. Dividing by the three examples gives 9.6667. Mean absolute error squares nothing, skipping the division reports the total rather than the mean, and adding in any residual uses the wrong sign, so those values are not the MSE.
questions.hint: Square each prediction-minus-target residual, add them, then divide by three.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply classification metrics to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: A classifier's confusion matrix reports 36 true positives, 6 false positives, and 1 false negatives. What is the F1 score for the positive class, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Reports recall and ignores precision
Uses a simplified accuracy that drops true negatives
Reports precision and ignores recall

questions.explanation: Precision is 36/(36+6) = 0.8571 and recall is 36/(36+1) = 0.973. The F1 score is their harmonic mean 2PR/(P+R) = 0.9114. Reporting precision or recall alone captures only one side of the tradeoff, and the simplified ratio is neither a harmonic mean nor the full accuracy.
questions.hint: Compute precision and recall, then take their harmonic mean.

questions.learningObjective: Apply linear regression to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Taking 6, 3 and 1 as the given figures, a linear regression model predicts with weights 6 and 3, and intercept 1. For an input with feature values x = 2 and y = 5, what value does the model predict?

options.misconception: Subtracts the intercept instead of adding it
Multiplies the features instead of weighting them
Omits the intercept term from the prediction

questions.explanation: A linear model computes the weighted sum plus the intercept: 6*2 + 3*5 + 1 = 12 + 15 + 1 = 28. Dropping the intercept, reversing its sign, or multiplying the features together all change the affine form that defines linear regression.
questions.hint: Multiply each feature by its weight, add the results, then add the intercept.
